pack.title: Unit 9.0 Evaluate Network Security Capabilities
pack.notes: Needs revision: written hands-off; Mr. Flauto has not checked it yet.

flashcards.definition: A collection of standard configurations and settings for areas such as network devices, software, patching, access controls, logging, and encryption, with consistent, centralized rules that improve security, manageability, and efficiency.
The step of defining the standard configurations a baseline will hold, usually built from published best-practice guides.
The step of pushing the baseline's settings out to many diverse systems, automated with configuration management tools so every system gets the same configuration.
The ongoing step of checking that systems still match the baseline and correcting any setting that drifts from it.

Improving a device's security by changing its default configuration, often by following a published secure baseline, because defaults with well-documented credentials, simple passwords, and insecure protocols attract attackers.

Network devices hardened from the list they share with routers (changing default credentials, SSH or HTTPS instead of Telnet or HTTP, ACLs), plus port security to limit which devices can connect to each of their ports.

Network devices hardened from the list they share with switches: change default credentials, turn off unneeded services like Telnet and HTTP, manage them over SSH or HTTPS, and limit who can reach them with ACLs.
Systems kept in racks or datacenters whose hardening adds regular patches, least privilege, antivirus, and firewalls and an IDS to the steps they share with switches and routers.

The factors that keep authorized Wi-Fi access points available, such as where each one is placed and which channel it uses, because patchy coverage leaves the network open to rogue and evil twin attacks.

Measuring signal strength and channel usage across the area to cover, starting from a map with interference sources marked, as a laptop or mobile device running Wi-Fi analyzer software records readings at regular points.
A color-coded picture built from site survey readings that shows where the signal is strong or weak and how channels overlap, used to adjust power, change channels, or add or move access points.
What a Wi-Fi network is configured with to protect it: a standard such as WPA2 or WPA3, which determines the encryption, how the key is made, and how devices authenticate when they join.
The wireless security standard that uses SAE in place of the pre-shared key exchange and the higher-performance AES GCM in place of AES CCM.
The standard for the AAA server that 802.1X typically uses to check the credentials of users or devices trying to connect.
The ciphers a Wi-Fi security standard supports so that no one in range can read the traffic, from RC4 in WEP and WPA to AES with CCM in WPA2 and AES with GCM in WPA3.
The ways a Wi-Fi network confirms only valid users join, in three types: personal (a passphrase, with PSK or SAE), open, and enterprise (each user's own credentials, through 802.1X).
The WPA2 personal method in which the access point and every device are set with the same passphrase.
The WPA3 personal method that replaces PSK and is designed to stop offline dictionary attacks on a captured handshake.
The enterprise-mode framework that lets a device onto the network only after it authenticates, with each user's own credentials checked by a server such as RADIUS instead of a shared passphrase.
A protocol with many types, each defining a specific way to check credentials, used with 802.1X and RADIUS in enterprise Wi-Fi.
The enterprise Wi-Fi method that uses certificates on both the client and the server, so each side proves its identity to the other (mutual authentication).
Turning on logging on switches, routers, and servers and keeping watch on it, to help spot issues such as repeated login failures and configuration changes.

A security system designed to protect a network's perimeter by stopping unauthorized access to or from it. It typically gives both network-level and application-level control over inbound and outbound traffic.

Entries telling a firewall to allow or block inbound or outbound traffic by address, port, protocol, or even an application's traffic pattern, read top to bottom and typically ending in an implicit deny.
A set of permissions tied to a network device, such as a router or switch, that permits or denies traffic at an interface by source and destination IP address, port number, and protocol.
Allowing or denying traffic by the TCP or UDP number a service runs on, such as letting only 80 and 443 (HTTP and HTTPS) reach a web server, or keeping FTP and SSH out when they are not needed.
A neutral zone that holds public-facing servers, such as web and email, apart from the internal network, to limit the damage if those servers are compromised.

A passive system that inspects traffic for potential threats, using predefined rules or unusual behavior, and alerts administrators without blocking anything, so false positives do not disrupt legitimate traffic.

A proactive system that spots threats in traffic and acts on them by blocking the offending source, dropping malicious packets, or resetting connections, which can stop damage at once but may block legitimate traffic on a false positive.
An IDS method in which the engine is loaded with a database of known attacks and raises an incident when traffic fits one of them; the database needs regular updates for the latest threats.

Tracking IDS and IPS events and alerts over time to spot patterns, such as a rise in alerts for one attack, and to find frequent false positives that can be tuned down so analysts can focus on more important alerts.

A control that analyzes browsing traffic, often in real time, and stops users from reaching malicious or inappropriate sites by URL, IP address, category, or keyword. Set too strict, it overblocks useful sites; too loose, it underblocks harmful ones.

Software installed on each desktop, laptop, and mobile device that gets browsing policies from a management server and applies them on the device itself, so they still work off the corporate network, such as at home.
An intermediary server that an organization routes its Internet traffic through, so it can permit or deny each web request by policy, log activity, anonymize requests, and cache content.
A proxy technique that examines the web address each user requests and stops specific addresses known to host malicious content, be inappropriate, or break the usage policy.
A proxy technique that classifies websites into groups, such as social networking, gambling, adult, and webmail, so rules can allow or deny a whole group at once.

A proxy technique that uses continually updated databases scoring websites on their observed behavior and history, so sites known for malware, phishing, or spam get a poor score and can be stopped automatically.

A system that authenticates users and devices and also checks that each meets security policy, such as its operating system version, patch level, and antivirus status, before it may connect, and can quarantine one that does not.

flashcards.term: User behavior analytics (user and entity behavior analytics, UEBA)
flashcards.definition: Machine-learning products that learn normal activity and flag anomalies, such as insider threats, using indicators from many intrusion detection and log sources, often integrated with a SIEM.
